questions.q: Which of these values is not a primitive?
questions.explain: The seven primitives are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. An array is an object: a mutable container with its own identity.

questions.q: Why does 10n + 1 throw a TypeError?
questions.explain: Mixing them would force JavaScript to pick a precision for you. Write 10n + 1n, 10n + BigInt(1) or Number(10n) + 1.
options: Because JavaScript refuses to mix bigint and number in arithmetic; you must convert one side explicitly
Because 1 is too small for a bigint
Because the n must come before the number

questions.q: What is special about a symbol?
questions.explain: Symbol("id") === Symbol("id") is false: the description is only a label. Symbol.for(name) is the exception, returning one shared symbol per name from a global registry.
options: It is a string that cannot be changed
Every Symbol() call creates a value equal only to itself, useful as a property key that cannot clash
It is a number with a name
It can only be used in the browser

questions.q: How do you check reliably whether a value is an array?
questions.explain: typeof says "object" for arrays, plain objects, dates and null alike. Array.isArray answers the question exactly; a string also has a length.

questions.q: When is a WeakMap the right choice?
questions.explain: A WeakMap accepts only objects as keys and does not keep them alive, so it cannot leak memory. In exchange you cannot iterate it or ask its size.
options: When you need to list all the entries later
When the keys are strings such as product codes
When you attach extra data to objects and want it forgotten automatically once the object is no longer used
When you need the number of entries

questions.q: After const template = { items: [] }; const cart = template; cart.items.push("Garri");, what is template.items?
questions.explain: Assignment copies the reference, not the object. There is one object with two names, so a change through either name is visible through both.
options: ["Garri"], because both names point at the same object

questions.q: A function does order = { total: 0 }; to its order parameter. What happens to the caller's object?
questions.explain: Parameters are new variables filled from the arguments. Reassigning one changes only that variable. Changing a property (order.total = 0) would change the caller's object, because both point at it.
options: It is replaced by the new object
Nothing: only the function's own variable now points at a new object

questions.q: Every new customer should start with an empty cart. Which approach gives each customer a separate cart?
questions.explain: An object literal creates a new object each time it runs, so a factory function that returns one gives every call its own cart and its own list inside.
options: const EMPTY = { items: [] }; and cart = EMPTY for each customer
A function createCart() that returns { items: [] }, called once per customer
Using let instead of const for the template

questions.q: Why does const cart = { items: [] }; cart.items.push("Oil"); work?
questions.explain: const is about the variable. cart = {} would fail, but changing the object it points at is allowed. To stop that, freeze the object.
options: Because const only stops the variable from being pointed at another value; the object itself can still change
It does not work: it throws a TypeError

questions.q: const config = Object.freeze({ vat: 7.5, limits: { daily: 100000 } }); Which change still succeeds?
questions.explain: Object.freeze is shallow: it locks the object's own properties, but limits is a separate object that was not frozen.

questions.q: What does const name = "ada"; name.toUpperCase(); do to name?
questions.explain: Primitives never change. String methods return new strings; to keep the result, store it: const loud = name.toUpperCase();.
options: Nothing: strings are immutable, and toUpperCase returns a new string that was not stored

questions.q: Why is { id: 1 } === { id: 1 } false?
questions.explain: For objects, === answers "is this the same object?". Two objects written separately are never the same object, whatever they contain.
options: Because === on objects checks identity, and these are two different objects

questions.q: You need to know whether two order-line objects have the same sku and qty. What is the most reliable check?
questions.explain: Nothing built in compares object contents. Compare the fields that matter. String(a) is "[object Object]" for every plain object, so it would call all of them equal.

questions.q: Which comparison is true?
questions.explain: Object.is is like === without its two exceptions: it treats NaN as equal to itself, and it tells 0 and -0 apart.

questions.q: Why does [NaN].indexOf(NaN) return -1 while [NaN].includes(NaN) returns true?
questions.explain: Different built-ins use different equality algorithms. includes, Map and Set use SameValueZero; indexOf uses strict equality.
options: Because indexOf compares with ===, and includes uses SameValueZero, which treats NaN as equal to NaN
It is a bug in V8

questions.q: Orders are stored in a Map with number keys. The id read from a web address is the string "42". What does orders.get("42") return?
questions.explain: Maps compare keys with SameValueZero, which never converts types. Convert the text to a number (after validating it) before the lookup.

questions.q: What decides whether + adds or joins text?
questions.explain: That is why 1 + 2 + "3" is "33" (first 3, then join) and "1" + 2 + 3 is "123".
options: The type of the left side only
After converting both sides to primitives, if either one is a string, it joins; otherwise it adds
Whether the values are in a template literal
It always adds, then converts to text

questions.q: Why is null >= 0 true while null == 0 is false?
questions.explain: Relational operators convert to numbers; loose equality has its own rule for null and undefined. Check for null explicitly instead of relying on either.
options: Because >= converts null to the number 0, while == never converts null: it only equals undefined
Because null is greater than zero

questions.q: Where should text from a form or web address be converted to numbers?
questions.explain: Converting at the edge means inner code never has to wonder whether an id is text, and invalid input is rejected in one place.
options: Wherever the value is used, each time
Once, where it enters the program, together with validation; the rest of the code receives real numbers
Nowhere: use == so the conversion happens automatically

questions.q: For which values is value == null true?
questions.explain: Loose equality makes null and undefined equal to each other and to nothing else. It is the one widely accepted use of ==.

questions.q: A customer email says: Your order [object Object] has shipped. What happened?
questions.explain: String conversion of a plain object uses its default toString. The template probably received the whole order object instead of order.id.
options: The order number was too long
An object was turned into text by accident, and a plain object's default text is "[object Object]"
The email service does not support numbers

questions.q: Which statement about typeof is correct?
questions.explain: For objects, typeof only distinguishes functions. Dates, arrays, maps and even null all give "object".
options: typeof function () {} is "function", although functions are objects

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: shopA is the same object as defaults, so the currency change shows up. shopB is a shallow copy: its own currency is separate, but tags still points at the same list.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The property change went to the caller's object. Reassigning the parameter only pointed the function's own variable at a new object, so the caller never sees note.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Empty text becomes 0 and spaces are trimmed, but any other character gives NaN. null becomes 0 and undefined NaN. Arrays become text first: "" is 0 and "8" is 8.
questions.code: console.log(Number(""), Number(" 7 "), Number("7kg"), Number(null), Number(undefined), Number([]), Number(["8"]));
options: 0 NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Arrays join their items with commas (an empty array is empty text), null becomes "null", a plain object becomes "[object Object]", and -0 loses its sign as text.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: + works left to right and joins as soon as one side is text. - always converts to numbers. true is 1. [] becomes "", so [] + 1 is the text "1". null is 0 in arithmetic.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Strings compared with numbers become numbers, so the first two are true, but two strings compare as text. A boolean becomes a number first: true is 1, so "2" == true is false. null only equals undefined.
options: true true false true false false
true true true true true false
false false false true false false
true true false true true true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: === treats NaN as unequal and 0/-0 as equal. Object.is does the opposite on both. includes uses SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, and 0 equals -0.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1 and "1" are different; the two NaNs count once; 0 and -0 count once (SameValueZero); the two objects are two different objects. 1, "1", NaN, 0 and two objects: 6.
questions.code:
const seen = new Set([1, "1", NaN, NaN, 0, -0, { id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]);
console.log(seen.size);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toSorted returns a new list. same is the same list as prices, and reverse changes that list in place, so prices is reversed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Arithmetic and comparisons ask for a number, so valueOf is used. A template literal prefers text, so toString is used.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: In strict code, writing to a frozen property throws a TypeError. Freezing is shallow, so the list inside can still grow.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: typeof names the primitive types, says "object" for null (the 1995 bug) and for every non-function object, and "function" for functions.
questions.code: console.log(typeof 5n, typeof Symbol(), typeof null, typeof [], typeof new Map(), typeof Math.max);
options: bigint symbol object object object function
number symbol null array map function
bigint symbol null object object function
bigint string object array object function

questions.q: All orders share one lines list because they all use the same template object. Replace the template with a factory function createOrder(id) that returns { id, lines: [] }, so each order is separate.
questions.explain: An object literal inside the function creates a new object, with a new list, on every call. The starter handed out one object, so the second call overwrote the id of the first.

questions.q: Write parsePage(text) for a page number from a web address: return the number if the text is only digits and the number is at least 1, otherwise return 1 (the first page).
questions.explain: Number("") would be 0 and Number(" 4") would be 4, so a digits-only check comes first. Everything invalid falls back to page 1, which is the decision this function documents.

questions.q: Write sameLine(a, b) that returns true when two order lines have the same sku and the same qty, whether or not they are the same object.
questions.explain: === on objects compares identity, so two equal-looking lines were "different". Comparing the fields that matter compares contents.

questions.q: Write withItem(cart, item) that returns a new cart object with item added to a new items list, leaving the original cart and its list unchanged.
questions.explain: [...cart.items, item] builds a new list from the old items plus the new one, and the braces build a new cart. The caller's cart is never changed.

questions.q: Amounts arrive from a CSV file as text. Write sumKobo(texts) that converts each one explicitly with Number() and returns the total, or null if any amount is not a whole number.
questions.explain: The starter joined text: 0 + "1500" is "01500". Converting each value explicitly makes + add numbers, and checking the result rejects decimals and NaN.

questions.q: Write kindOf(value) that returns "null" for null, "array" for arrays, "date" for dates, and typeof value for everything else.
questions.explain: typeof says "object" for null, arrays and dates. Check null with ===, arrays with Array.isArray and dates with instanceof before falling back to typeof.
questions.expected: null array date object string bigint function

questions.q: Prices arrive as text. Return a new list of them as numbers, sorted from cheapest to most expensive, without changing the original list.
questions.explain: Sorted as text, "10000" comes before "200", and sort changes the caller's list. Converting to numbers and using toSorted with a - b fixes both.

questions.q: Some ids arrive as numbers and some as text. Write distinctIds(ids) that returns how many different ids there are, treating 42 and "42" as the same id. Use a Set.
questions.explain: A Set compares with SameValueZero, which never converts types, so 42 and "42" were counted twice. Converting every id to one type first makes the Set compare like with like.
